Pain and Suffering Damages in Washington: What They Cover, Who Decides, and Why There Is No Formula

Justin D. Leigh, Attorney-at-Law·7 min read·November 11, 2026

Six months after the crash your medical bills are paid, you are back at work, and the adjuster writes that what is left of your claim is "general damages." Your knee still aches on stairs, you stopped coaching your daughter's team, and you wake at three in the morning replaying the intersection. None of that comes with a receipt, and the adjuster's number reads like a guess. In Washington the amount is a question of fact for a jury, and the state Supreme Court has held that the Legislature cannot cut it down by formula.

What counts as pain and suffering?

Lawyers call it noneconomic damages, and the term is broader than physical pain. Washington damages in an injury case divide into two kinds. Economic damages are the losses with a dollar figure attached: medical bills, lost wages, the cost of replacing what you can no longer do yourself. Noneconomic damages are everything else the injury took.

The clearest list Washington has written comes from a statute that no longer exists. Former RCW 4.56.250, as quoted by the Supreme Court in Sofie v. Fibreboard Corp., 112 Wn.2d 636 (1989), defined noneconomic damages as "subjective, nonmonetary losses, including, but not limited to pain, suffering, inconvenience, mental anguish, disability or disfigurement incurred by the injured party, emotional distress, loss of society and companionship, loss of consortium, injury to reputation and humiliation, and destruction of the parent-child relationship." The section is gone, for reasons below, but the list is still a good inventory of what an injury can cost a person.

Some of those losses belong to people other than the one who was hurt. Loss of consortium is a spouse's claim for what the injury did to the marriage. Destruction of the parent-child relationship is a loss to the family. When someone is seriously injured, the question of whose losses are in the case deserves an answer early.

Is there a cap on pain and suffering damages in Washington?

There was one, and the Supreme Court struck it down. In 1986 the Legislature passed RCW 4.56.250 as part of a tort reform act. As the court described it in Sofie, the limit worked on a formula tied to the plaintiff's age, so the older the plaintiff, the less he or she could recover. The jury decided noneconomic damages without being told the limit existed, and the judge then reduced any verdict that exceeded it.

In Sofie, a jury had awarded damages to a man dying of mesothelioma caused by asbestos exposure and to his wife for her loss of consortium. The trial judge found the award reasonable but reduced it under the statute. The Supreme Court held that "the statute's damages limit interferes with the jury's traditional function to determine damages" and that RCW 4.56.250 therefore violated article 1, section 21 of the Washington Constitution, which protects the right to a jury as inviolate. The court said the limit "is no longer operative" and reinstated the jury's award.

The section has since been taken out of the code. The Legislature's disposition table records RCW 4.56.250 as repealed by 2023 c 102 s 5. So the general limit on noneconomic damages in Washington is gone, both as a matter of constitutional law and as a matter of what the statute books say. That is not the same as saying a claim has no ceiling. In practice the ceiling is often the insurance available, which is a reason to find every policy early.

Who decides how much pain and suffering is worth?

A jury, if the case is tried to one. Sofie rests on the principle that the amount of damages is a question of fact, and that finding facts is the jury's job. The court quoted its own earlier statement: "The determination of the amount of damages, particularly in actions of this nature, is primarily and peculiarly within the province of the jury, under proper instructions ..."

The jury is instructed on the kinds of harm it may consider and is then left to its own judgment about amount, guided by the evidence. There is no schedule or chart it applies. Different juries can reach different numbers on similar injuries, and the system accepts that as the cost of letting ordinary people decide what a loss is worth.

The trial judge keeps a check on the result. Sofie acknowledged that trial judges have the power of remittitur, which allows a judge to reduce a verdict, and distinguished it from the statute: remittitur is a judicial conclusion reached in a particular case, while the cap operated automatically on every verdict above a formula. That distinction is the reason a judge may still review an award that a statute could not cut.

How do you prove pain and suffering without a receipt?

With specifics, and with witnesses other than yourself. A jury is asked to put a value on something it cannot see, so the evidence has to make it visible.

Medical records matter more than people expect, and not only for the bills. A chart that records pain at every visit, the medications tried, and the activities you said you could no longer do is evidence written at the time by someone with no stake in the lawsuit. A treating provider who can say what is permanent, and what the future looks like, carries the claim forward past the trial date.

The people around you are the next layer. A spouse, a coworker, a friend from the team you no longer play on can describe who you were before and what changed, in terms a juror recognizes. Photographs of the injury during recovery, and of the life you had before it, do the same work. A simple journal kept during recovery can help you remember accurately what you went through months later, when you are asked about it under oath.

What does not work is generality. "I am in pain" persuades nobody. "I can no longer pick up my son" does.

Is there a formula or multiplier for pain and suffering?

Not in Washington law. No statute or case sets a multiple of medical bills or a figure per day. The Legislature did write one, the age-based limit in former RCW 4.56.250, and the Supreme Court held it unconstitutional because it substituted a calculation for the jury's judgment.

Rules of thumb circulate anyway, and an adjuster may use one in negotiation. A number produced that way is a negotiating position, not a measure of your loss, and it tends to undervalue exactly the injuries this category exists for: the ones with modest bills and lasting effects on how a person lives.

Does my own share of fault reduce pain and suffering?

Yes, in proportion, and it does not end the claim. RCW 4.22.005 provides that contributory fault chargeable to the claimant "diminishes proportionately the amount awarded as compensatory damages" but "does not bar recovery." Noneconomic damages are compensatory damages, so if a jury finds you partly at fault, the award for pain and suffering is reduced by your percentage along with everything else.

Fault is defined broadly. RCW 4.22.015 includes the "unreasonable failure to avoid an injury or to mitigate damages." That is how skipped appointments, ignored medical advice, or a long gap in treatment can turn into a percentage against you, and it is one more reason the medical record matters.

Pain and suffering when the injured person has died

The claim does not disappear. RCW 4.20.046(2) allows the personal representative of the estate to recover noneconomic damages for the "pain and suffering, anxiety, emotional distress, or humiliation personal to and suffered by the deceased," on behalf of the beneficiaries listed in RCW 4.20.020. That is separate from the family's own losses in a wrongful death claim, and the two are proved with different evidence. The article on wrongful death covers both.

Where this goes wrong

The claim settles before treatment is finished, so the noneconomic damages are valued before anyone knows whether the injury is permanent.

The medical records say almost nothing about pain or limitations, because nobody told the patient that what they report at appointments becomes the evidence.

A gap in treatment, whatever the reason, is read as recovery and then as a failure to mitigate.

Social media shows a smiling photograph from a good day, and it becomes the defense's exhibit about every other day.

The spouse's loss of consortium claim is never raised, and the case settles without anyone accounting for it.

The injured person describes the harm in general terms and the jury never hears the details that would have made it real.

What a lawyer does here

Most of the work on noneconomic damages is building a record that a stranger can understand. Making sure the treating providers document what the injury actually does, not just what it is. Finding the witnesses who knew you before and can describe the difference. Getting an opinion on permanency before any number is discussed. Identifying every person in the family who has a claim of their own. Finding every policy that might pay. And giving you a straight answer about comparative fault, because a reduction you see coming is easier to plan for than one that arrives in the verdict.
